item.content:encoded:
As many accomplished professionals approach the next stage of their careers, a common question emerges: How can decades of expertise, leadership, and experience be applied to create lasting change in society? Georgetown University’s Fellowship for the Common Good was created to help answer that question.

The Fellowship for the Common Good is an innovative, year-long, in-person fellowship program designed for highly experienced professionals who want to redirect their knowledge, skills, and influence toward addressing some of society’s most pressing challenges. Hosted by Georgetown University in Washington, D.C., the fellowship combines academic learning, personal reflection, policy engagement, mentorship, and practical action planning to help participants create a lasting legacy through service and leadership.

Launching its inaugural cohort in August 2027, this unique program brings together seasoned leaders from diverse sectors to explore purpose-driven work while developing actionable solutions to societal issues that matter most to them.

Why the Georgetown Fellowship for the Common Good Stands Out

Unlike traditional academic programs that focus solely on professional advancement, the Fellowship for the Common Good is designed specifically for professionals with substantial career experience who are considering how to use their expertise in ways that benefit communities, institutions, and society at large.

The program encourages participants to reflect deeply on questions of purpose, ethics, leadership, and legacy while simultaneously engaging with real-world policy issues and social challenges.

At the heart of the fellowship is a simple but profound idea: successful careers can become platforms for creating lasting societal impact.

Program Overview

The Georgetown University Fellowship for the Common Good is:

  • A year-long fellowship program
  • Delivered fully in person
  • Located in Washington, D.C.
  • Designed for professionals with more than 20 years of work experience
  • Structured around academic coursework, policy engagement, mentorship, and project development

Participants work closely with Georgetown faculty, policy experts, scholars, and peers from diverse professional backgrounds throughout the year.

A Curriculum Built Around Purpose and Impact

The fellowship centers on two concurrent core courses that guide participants through an exploration of purpose, leadership, ethics, and societal change.

The curriculum helps fellows:

  • Reflect on their personal and professional journeys
  • Examine broader questions of purpose and meaning
  • Develop frameworks for ethical leadership
  • Identify societal challenges they are passionate about addressing
  • Design sustainable approaches for achieving impact

In addition to the core coursework, fellows can audit select Georgetown University courses based on their interests and goals, allowing them to deepen their knowledge in specific subject areas.

This flexibility enables each participant to tailor part of the learning experience to align with their personal mission and future aspirations.

The Purpose Plan: Turning Vision into Action

One of the most distinctive features of the fellowship is the creation of a Purpose Plan.

Throughout the year, fellows develop a customized action plan focused on a societal issue they care about. Rather than ending the program with only ideas and reflections, participants leave with a practical roadmap designed to help them create real-world impact.

The Purpose Plan includes:

  • Identification of a social issue of interest
  • Strategic objectives
  • Practical implementation steps
  • Long-term impact goals
  • Personal leadership commitments

This action-oriented approach ensures that learning translates into meaningful community, national, or global contributions.

Exclusive Access to Policymakers and Experts

Being located in the nation’s capital provides unparalleled opportunities for engagement with influential leaders and decision-makers.

Fellows participate in exclusive policy briefings and discussions with:

  • Policymakers
  • Government leaders
  • Academic scholars
  • Public policy experts
  • Thought leaders
  • Researchers

The program provides direct exposure to contemporary issues affecting society, governance, public service, democracy, sustainability, ethics, and social justice.

These briefings allow participants to gain firsthand insights into the challenges and opportunities shaping public life today.

Areas of Focus and Study

The fellowship allows participants to explore issues that align with their expertise and passions.

Potential areas of interest include:

Public Health

Participants can explore pressing healthcare challenges, health equity, access to care, and public policy initiatives that improve societal well-being.

Sustainability and Environmental Issues

Fellows interested in environmental stewardship can engage with sustainability initiatives, climate-related issues, and conservation strategies.

Global Affairs and International Relations

The program offers opportunities to examine global challenges, diplomacy, international development, and cross-border cooperation.

Education Reform

Professionals committed to improving educational outcomes can explore strategies for advancing educational access, quality, and innovation.

Affordable Housing

Participants may investigate ways to address housing shortages, affordability concerns, and community development challenges.

Ethics and Civic Leadership

The fellowship provides opportunities to study ethical decision-making and responsible leadership in public and private institutions.

Racial Justice and Social Equity

Fellows can engage with discussions surrounding equity, inclusion, and social justice while exploring practical solutions for positive change.

Learning Through Intergenerational Engagement

A distinctive aspect of the Fellowship for the Common Good is its emphasis on intergenerational learning.

Participants have opportunities to mentor Georgetown students while also learning from younger generations.

This exchange creates valuable dialogue between experienced professionals and emerging leaders, fostering:

  • Knowledge sharing
  • Professional development
  • Leadership growth
  • Broader societal understanding
  • Cross-generational collaboration

Guided by Georgetown’s Jesuit Tradition

The fellowship is deeply inspired by Georgetown University’s Jesuit mission.

This educational tradition emphasizes:

  • Reflection
  • Service
  • Ethical leadership
  • Personal growth
  • Social responsibility
  • Care for the whole person

Importantly, Georgetown welcomes individuals from all religious, cultural, and professional backgrounds. The fellowship is designed to be inclusive and accessible to people regardless of faith tradition, encouraging participants to integrate the program’s values in ways that align with their personal beliefs and life experiences.

Program Objectives

The fellowship aims to help participants transition into their next chapter of leadership and impact.

During the program, fellows will:

  1. Learn strategies for addressing societal challenges.
  2. Explore questions of meaning and purpose.
  3. Pursue intellectual growth.
  4. Strengthen ethical decision-making frameworks.
  5. Collaborate with accomplished professionals from diverse fields.
  6. Participate in intergenerational learning through student mentorship.
  7. Develop a comprehensive Purpose Plan for future impact.

Distinguished Faculty and Leadership

The Fellowship for the Common Good is led by Professor Melissa L. Bradley, a renowned expert whose career spans entrepreneurship, public policy, investment, business leadership, and education.

With experience in both the Clinton and Obama administrations, Professor Bradley has spent decades supporting entrepreneurs, developing ventures, leading investment funds, and teaching future leaders.

Her leadership helps ensure that the fellowship combines academic rigor with practical real-world relevance.

Participants also benefit from engagement with distinguished Georgetown scholars and experts, including leaders in:

  • Public policy
  • Democracy studies
  • Ethics
  • Sustainability
  • Environmental research
  • Social impact initiatives

Study in the Heart of Washington, D.C.

The fellowship takes place at Georgetown University’s Capitol Campus, one of the most strategically located academic settings in the United States.

Core classes are hosted at:

111 Mass Avenue NW, Washington, D.C.

The location places fellows within walking distance of:

  • The U.S. Capitol
  • Georgetown Law
  • The McCourt School of Public Policy
  • Government institutions
  • Major policy organizations
  • National think tanks

Participants also receive dedicated workspace access during the program, creating an immersive environment for learning, collaboration, and project development.

Benefits of Joining the Fellowship

By participating in the Fellowship for the Common Good, fellows gain:

  • Access to Georgetown University’s world-class faculty
  • Direct engagement with policymakers and scholars
  • A structured environment for purposeful reflection
  • Opportunities for personalized learning
  • Intergenerational mentorship experiences
  • Exposure to diverse societal issues
  • A collaborative network of highly experienced peers
  • A practical Purpose Plan for long-term impact
  • Access to resources in the nation’s capital

Qualifications

  • Minimum of 20 years of professional work experience
  • Demonstrated interest in addressing societal issues
  • Commitment to active participation in a year-long, in-person program
  • Willingness to engage in mentorship, reflection, academic learning, and collaborative discussions

Application Timeline

Important Date

  • Inaugural Fellowship Cohort Launch: August 2027

The program welcomes conversations and inquiries from prospective fellows interested in future enrollment opportunities.

Application Deadline: Apply as soon as possible

APPLY  HERE:

For more information about the Fellowship for the Common Good, CLICK HERE.

Conclusion

The Georgetown University Fellowship for the Common Good represents a unique opportunity for accomplished professionals to transform decades of experience into meaningful social impact. Rather than focusing solely on career advancement, the fellowship challenges participants to think deeply about purpose, legacy, and the role they can play in addressing society’s most significant challenges.

Through rigorous academic engagement, policy immersion, mentorship opportunities, interdisciplinary collaboration, and the development of a personalized Purpose Plan, fellows gain the tools needed to create sustained and measurable change. For professionals seeking a thoughtful transition into a purpose-driven chapter of life, the Fellowship for the Common Good offers an exceptional platform to learn, reflect, and act.

item.content:encoded:
The Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship 2026 is an opportunity for young women with backgrounds in Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics (STEM) to develop their teaching, leadership and professional skills while contributing to improved secondary education in Uganda.

Implemented by Teach For Uganda under the Leaders in Teaching Program, the STEM Fellowship is designed to address the need for more capable, committed and well-supported STEM teachers in Uganda, with a particular emphasis on increasing the participation and leadership of women in STEM education.

The pilot programme is supported by the Mastercard Foundation and implemented through a consortium led by the Luigi Giussani Foundation and other education partners.

The fellowship combines classroom teaching, professional development, coaching and leadership development. Fellows are placed in secondary schools and supported to become effective teachers, mentors and role models for learners, particularly girls who may face barriers to participating confidently in STEM subjects.

What Is the Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship?

The Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship is a pilot programme focused on strengthening STEM teaching in Uganda’s secondary schools.

The programme recognises that Science, Technology, Engineering and Mathematics are increasingly important to education, employment, innovation and national development. However, access to quality STEM education remains uneven, particularly for learners in underserved communities.

The fellowship therefore seeks to recruit young people with strong STEM backgrounds and develop them into teachers and education leaders.

Participants are not simply placed in classrooms and expected to teach independently. The fellowship provides structured preparation, coaching and continuous professional development to help Fellows build the skills required to become effective educators.

The programme also creates a pathway for young women with STEM backgrounds to enter education, take on leadership responsibilities and become visible role models for girls interested in science and technology.

Why STEM Education Matters in Uganda

STEM subjects play an increasingly important role in preparing young people for a changing world.

Science, technology, engineering and mathematics influence how people:

  • Understand the world around them
  • Solve complex problems
  • Develop new technologies
  • Create businesses and employment opportunities
  • Respond to social and environmental challenges
  • Participate in the future workforce
  • Develop innovative solutions
  • Contribute to national development

Despite the importance of STEM education, many learners continue to encounter barriers that affect their participation and confidence.

Girls in underserved communities can face additional challenges, including limited access to role models and learning environments that encourage them to pursue STEM-related opportunities.

The Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship seeks to address some of these challenges by bringing more talented STEM graduates and young professionals into secondary-school classrooms.

Through effective teaching and mentorship, Fellows can help learners understand that STEM is not simply about memorising formulas or concepts. Instead, STEM can be practical, creative and connected to real-world challenges.

A Focus on Girls and Women in STEM

One of the distinctive aspects of the STEM Fellowship is its emphasis on increasing the participation and visibility of young women in STEM education.

The programme recognises that representation matters.

When girls encounter women who are teaching science, mathematics and other STEM-related subjects, they can see examples of women actively participating in fields that have historically had gender-related participation gaps.

The fellowship therefore seeks to create opportunities for young women to:

  • Teach STEM subjects
  • Become classroom leaders
  • Mentor learners
  • Encourage girls to participate in STEM
  • Serve as positive role models
  • Develop their own leadership abilities
  • Contribute to education reform and community change

The broader goal is to strengthen both the teacher pipeline and the participation of girls in STEM learning.

About the STEM Fellowship Pilot

The STEM Fellowship operates as an intentional pilot under the Leaders in Teaching Program.

As a pilot, the programme provides Teach For Uganda with an opportunity to test the effectiveness of a leadership-focused fellowship model within secondary STEM education.

The organisation can use lessons and evidence generated through the programme to understand:

  • How STEM teachers can be effectively recruited
  • How new teachers can be prepared for classroom responsibilities
  • What types of coaching and professional development are useful
  • How leadership development can strengthen teaching
  • How STEM learning can become more learner-centred
  • How girls’ participation in STEM can be encouraged
  • How the fellowship model could potentially be strengthened and expanded

The pilot is therefore not only intended to benefit individual Fellows. It is also designed to generate learning that can contribute to longer-term improvements in Uganda’s education system.

What Fellows Will Do

STEM Fellows will be placed in secondary schools where they will contribute directly to teaching and learner development.

Their responsibilities and experience are expected to involve more than delivering lessons.

Fellows will be supported to develop classrooms where learners can:

  • Ask questions
  • Explore ideas
  • Test concepts
  • Solve problems
  • Connect classroom learning with real-life situations
  • Develop confidence
  • Become more curious about STEM
  • Participate actively in the learning process

The programme encourages Fellows to use learner-centred and inquiry-based approaches rather than relying exclusively on memorisation.

Training, Coaching and Professional Development

A key component of the fellowship is professional preparation and ongoing support.

Fellows receive structured training, coaching and continuous professional development to help them grow into effective educators.

This support is intended to help Fellows strengthen both their technical knowledge and their teaching abilities.

Areas of development include:

  • Classroom leadership
  • STEM teaching
  • Learner-centred education
  • Inquiry-based learning
  • Professional growth
  • Leadership
  • Mentorship
  • Community engagement
  • Problem-solving
  • Education equity

This combination makes the fellowship a leadership-development pathway as well as a teaching programme.

One-Year Postgraduate Diploma in Education

Successful Fellows must be willing to undertake a one-year, fully funded Postgraduate Diploma in Education (PGDE) during their first year of enrolment.

This is an important part of the professional development pathway.

The PGDE can provide Fellows with formal training in education and pedagogy while they develop their practical experience as teachers.

Because the programme specifies that the PGDE is fully funded, Fellows who meet the programme requirements do not have to pay for this training themselves.

The Teach For Uganda Approach

Teach For Uganda views teaching as a form of leadership.

Under the STEM Fellowship, this philosophy means that teachers are expected to combine strong subject knowledge with:

  • Classroom leadership
  • Creativity
  • Commitment to learner development
  • Community engagement
  • Problem-solving
  • Continuous learning
  • Advocacy for education equity

The programme aims to develop teachers who can influence not only what happens during individual lessons but also how learners perceive themselves and their future opportunities.

Learner-Centred STEM Teaching

The fellowship promotes learner-centred approaches to STEM education.

Instead of positioning learners as passive recipients of information, Fellows are encouraged to create classrooms where students actively participate in the learning process.

This can include encouraging students to:

  1. Ask questions about concepts they encounter.
  2. Investigate problems.
  3. Test ideas.
  4. Explore possible solutions.
  5. Connect academic concepts with everyday experiences.
  6. Work through challenges.
  7. Develop confidence in their ability to solve problems.

Such an approach can help make STEM learning more practical and engaging.

Community-Based Leadership

The fellowship also encourages Fellows to contribute to community-rooted solutions that can improve learning.

This reflects the programme’s broader leadership philosophy.

Rather than viewing education challenges only from inside the classroom, Fellows are encouraged to understand the communities they serve and consider how local circumstances influence educational outcomes.

This can help Fellows develop leadership skills that extend beyond traditional teaching responsibilities.

What Makes the STEM Fellowship Different?

The programme identifies several areas that distinguish the STEM Fellowship.

1. STEM Subject Focus

The fellowship is specifically designed to strengthen teaching in science and mathematics-related areas and develop a stronger pipeline of STEM educators.

2. Girls’ Leadership

The programme places particular emphasis on creating pathways for young women to enter STEM teaching and become leaders and role models.

3. Classroom Impact

Fellows are prepared to improve how STEM subjects are taught and experienced by learners.

4. Leadership Development

The fellowship aims to develop leaders who can contribute to education change beyond their immediate classroom responsibilities.

5. Systems Learning

Because the programme is a pilot, Teach For Uganda intends to learn from the experience and use evidence from the initiative to inform future development and potential expansion of the model.

Who Is Teach For Uganda Looking For?

The programme is looking for young leaders who believe education can contribute to Uganda’s future.

Ideal candidates should demonstrate a combination of STEM knowledge, leadership potential and commitment to education equity.

Teach For Uganda highlights candidates who are:

  • Passionate about education equity
  • Strong in STEM knowledge
  • Willing to develop their teaching abilities
  • Committed to supporting learners
  • Particularly interested in supporting girls in STEM
  • Open to coaching and constructive feedback
  • Committed to continuous learning
  • Willing to teach in secondary schools
  • Flexible about school placement
  • Interested in contributing to broader education change
  • Ready to serve underserved communities

The programme is particularly committed to developing pathways for young women with STEM backgrounds.

VISIT HERE, for more imformation.

Eligibility Requirements for the Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship

Applicants must meet the mandatory eligibility requirements set by the programme.

1. Ugandan Citizenship or Refugee Status

Applicants must be either:

  • A female Ugandan citizen, or
  • A refugee currently residing in Uganda.

This means the programme is not presented as an open international fellowship for applicants from other countries.

2. Bachelor’s Degree in a STEM Field

Applicants must hold a Bachelor’s degree in a STEM field.

The degree must have been completed with a minimum CGPA of 3.0.

Applicants should therefore have an academic background that is relevant to Science, Technology, Engineering or Mathematics.

3. Age Requirement

Applicants must be between 22 and 27 years old at the time of application.

Candidates outside this age range would not meet the stated mandatory age criterion.

4. English Language Proficiency

Applicants must be proficient in English.

English proficiency is important because Fellows will teach in secondary-school classrooms and participate in training and professional development.

5. Flexibility on School Placement

Applicants must be willing to be placed in any USE (Universal Secondary Education) secondary school.

This means candidates should be prepared to serve in the school location assigned to them rather than requiring placement in a particular school or area.

Flexibility regarding placement is therefore an important part of the fellowship.

6. Commitment to Education Equity and Leadership

Applicants should demonstrate a genuine interest in:

  • Education equity
  • Leadership
  • Community change
  • Supporting learners
  • STEM education
  • Girls’ participation in STEM

The programme is intended for candidates who want to contribute to educational improvement rather than simply obtain teaching experience.

7. Willingness to Undertake the PGDE

Applicants must be willing to undertake the one-year, fully funded Postgraduate Diploma in Education during their first year of enrolment.

This is a mandatory component of the programme.

Benefits of the Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship

The fellowship provides several professional and educational benefits to successful participants.

Fully Funded Postgraduate Education

Fellows are supported to undertake a one-year Postgraduate Diploma in Education during their first year.

The PGDE is described as fully funded under the fellowship.

Teaching Experience

Participants gain practical experience teaching in secondary schools.

This can help STEM graduates develop real-world classroom experience and understand the responsibilities involved in education.

Professional Development

Fellows receive training, coaching and continuous professional development.

This gives participants opportunities to strengthen their teaching and leadership skills over time.

Leadership Development

The fellowship is structured as a leadership pathway.

Participants are expected to develop skills that can help them contribute to education and community change beyond their classroom roles.

Mentorship and Coaching

Ongoing coaching and support provide Fellows with guidance as they transition into teaching and develop professionally.

Opportunity to Inspire Girls

Women participating in the fellowship have the opportunity to become visible STEM role models for girls in secondary schools.

This can contribute to broader efforts to encourage girls to develop confidence and interest in science and technology.

Contribution to Education Equity

Fellows serve in secondary-school settings, including underserved communities, allowing them to contribute directly to efforts aimed at improving educational opportunities.

Participation in a Broader Education Movement

The STEM Fellowship forms part of Teach For Uganda’s wider work to advance equitable access to quality education.

Fellows therefore become part of a broader movement focused on education leadership and systemic change.

Leaders in Teaching Program

The STEM Fellowship is implemented under the Leaders in Teaching Program, a flagship initiative supported by the Mastercard Foundation.

The programme is implemented through a consortium led by the Luigi Giussani Foundation.

The Leaders in Teaching Program brings together education partners working to strengthen secondary education through areas such as:

  • Teacher recruitment
  • Teacher training
  • Leadership development
  • Teacher motivation
  • Professional support
  • System-level education support

Teach For Uganda’s contribution focuses on strengthening the teacher pipeline by recruiting, preparing and mentoring STEM teachers who demonstrate both subject mastery and leadership potential.

Teach For Uganda’s Role

Teach For Uganda brings more than a decade of experience in leadership development and classroom placement to the STEM Fellowship pilot.

Through this initiative, the organisation is applying its experience to the specific challenge of strengthening secondary STEM education.

The programme therefore represents an expansion of Teach For Uganda’s work into secondary education and a deeper focus on STEM teaching and girls’ education.

Vision for the STEM Fellowship Pilot

Teach For Uganda describes the STEM Fellowship as the beginning of an important shift in its work.

The initiative expands the organisation’s focus into:

  • Secondary education
  • STEM education
  • Girls’ education
  • Women’s leadership
  • Teacher development
  • Education systems strengthening

The organisation aims to learn from the pilot, strengthen the model and potentially develop pathways that can support more learners, schools and communities over time.

The broader vision is based on the idea that improving education depends not only on getting children into school but also on the quality of learning, the people leading that learning and the opportunities learners can envision for themselves.

Is the STEM Fellowship Free?

Yes.

Teach For Uganda states that all services provided under the STEM Fellowship are free of charge.

There are no fees associated with:

  • Registration
  • Training
  • Scholarships
  • Other services provided through the programme

Applicants should therefore be cautious of anyone claiming to represent the programme and requesting payment for registration or participation.

For questions or concerns about the STEM Fellowship, Teach For Uganda provides the recruitment contact:

Email: recruitment@teachforuganda.org

How to Apply for the Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship

Interested and eligible applicants should submit their applications through the official application portal provided by Teach For Uganda.

The application link provided by the programme is:

APPLY HERE.

Applicants should ensure that they meet all mandatory eligibility requirements before submitting an application.

In particular, prospective candidates should verify their:

  1. Ugandan citizenship or refugee status in Uganda
  2. Female eligibility requirement
  3. STEM Bachelor’s degree
  4. Minimum CGPA of 3.0
  5. Age between 22 and 27
  6. English proficiency
  7. Willingness to accept placement in any USE secondary school
  8. Commitment to education equity and leadership
  9. Willingness to undertake the fully funded one-year PGDE

Important Application Information

The fellowship is specifically designed around the needs of Uganda’s secondary education system.

Applicants should therefore understand that this is not simply a general graduate scholarship or academic fellowship.

Successful participants will be expected to engage with teaching, classroom leadership, professional development and community service.

The requirement to be flexible about school placement is particularly important for applicants who may be considering the programme from outside the location where they currently live.

Conclusion

The Teach For Uganda STEM Fellowship 2026 provides a structured pathway for young women with STEM backgrounds to enter secondary education, develop teaching and leadership skills, and contribute to improving STEM learning in Uganda.

The fellowship combines classroom placement with training, coaching, professional development and a fully funded one-year Postgraduate Diploma in Education. It also places a strong emphasis on girls’ participation in STEM by creating opportunities for women to become teachers, mentors and role models.

As a pilot under the Leaders in Teaching Program, the initiative also has a broader systems-level purpose. Teach For Uganda aims to learn from the fellowship and use evidence from the programme to strengthen the teacher pipeline and inform future approaches to secondary STEM education.

For eligible candidates who are passionate about education equity, STEM, leadership and community change, the fellowship provides an opportunity to develop professionally while contributing directly to Uganda’s education sector.

Prospective applicants should carefully review the eligibility requirements and submit their application through the official application portal when applications are open. The programme states that participation and all associated services are free of charge.

The Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 is now accepting applications from experienced professionals whose work is focused on improving the built and natural environment and creating meaningful social impact. Hosted through the Harvard Graduate School of Design (GSD), the Fellowship is designed for mid-career practitioners who want to step back from their regular professional responsibilities, reflect on their experience, develop new skills, explore ideas, and prepare for the next stage of their careers.

For the 2027–28 Fellowship year, applications are open until Tuesday, January 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. Eastern Time (ET). There is no application fee, and international candidates are encouraged to apply.

The Loeb Fellowship is particularly distinctive because it is not structured as a conventional academic fellowship, artist residency, or sabbatical program. Instead, it is designed for established practitioners who are already active in their professions and who have demonstrated the ability to contribute to their fields and communities.

What Is the Harvard Loeb Fellowship?

The Loeb Fellowship is a mid-career professional development opportunity associated with Harvard University’s Graduate School of Design. It brings experienced practitioners into an environment where they can reassess what they have learned, expand their capabilities, engage with new ideas, and plan the next stage of their professional work.

The program is aimed at individuals whose professional activities involve designing, planning, preserving, developing, critiquing, or otherwise influencing the places and environments in which people live, work, and interact.

The Fellowship recognizes that improving the built and natural environment requires contributions from many different professional disciplines. Consequently, applicants do not have to be architects or designers to be considered.

The program specifically identifies professionals such as:

  • Urban designers
  • Public artists
  • Developers
  • Journalists
  • Civic leaders
  • Architects
  • Landscape architects
  • Urban planners
  • Policymakers
  • Community development leaders

The Fellowship also has a broad understanding of professional practice and social impact. Previous or potential applicants may come from less traditional backgrounds, including fields such as theatre, documentary filmmaking, journalism, and public art.

Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 Deadline

The application deadline for the 2027–28 Harvard Loeb Fellowship is January 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

Applicants should pay close attention to the deadline because the recommendation letters have a separate deadline.

Key deadlines include:

  • Main application deadline: Tuesday, January 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET
  • Recommendation deadline: Tuesday, January 12, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET
  • Loeb Connect participation request deadline: November 30, 2026, for applicants planning to apply for the 2027–28 class

The Fellowship advises applicants to begin working on their applications and recommendations well before the final deadline. Recommendation requests can be initiated before the applicant has completed the entire application.

Who Should Apply for the Harvard Loeb Fellowship?

The Fellowship is designed for mid-career professionals, rather than students or people who are just beginning their careers.

Applicants are expected to have a minimum of eight years of professional experience in their field.

The program is looking for practitioners who demonstrate:

  • Exceptional professional skill
  • Leadership ability
  • A commitment to helping others succeed
  • A strong record of professional work
  • A desire to make a meaningful difference in their field
  • The potential to develop their abilities further
  • An interest in improving the built or natural environment
  • The capacity to use the Fellowship experience to make a broader impact

The program notes that a typical Loeb class averages approximately 42 years of age, but the stated eligibility requirement is based on professional experience and the applicant’s stage of career rather than a specific age limit.

You Do Not Need to Be an Architect or Designer

One of the important features of the Harvard Loeb Fellowship is its broad definition of professional practice.

Applicants do not necessarily have to identify as designers. The Fellowship has previously welcomed professionals working across different disciplines, including public artists, journalists, theatre directors, documentary filmmakers, architects, landscape architects, and urban planners.

The central consideration is whether the applicant’s work contributes to improving the built or natural environment and has broader social impact.

Therefore, professionals with interdisciplinary or unconventional careers should not automatically assume that they are ineligible simply because their job title does not correspond to a traditional design profession.

Is a University Degree Required?

No.

A completed higher-education degree is not a requirement for admission to the Loeb Fellowship.

The Fellowship states that it values a creative and motivated work history and a commitment to supporting others over more traditional credentials. Professionals with unusual career paths or atypical backgrounds are encouraged to apply if they have demonstrated the ability to make a difference in their fields.

Applicants who have obtained university degrees may include their educational information in their resumes, but applicants are not required to have a degree in order to apply.

The program also states that it does not review academic transcripts.

Are International Applicants Eligible?

Yes.

The Harvard Loeb Fellowship is not restricted to U.S. citizens. International candidates are specifically encouraged to apply.

Successful international applicants will need to obtain a J-1 visa and must therefore be eligible to obtain the appropriate visa at the time of selection.

This makes the Fellowship accessible to qualified practitioners from outside the United States, provided they satisfy the program’s professional requirements and can meet the applicable visa requirements if selected.

What Is the Loeb Fellowship Looking For?

The Fellowship is designed for professionals who are at an important stage in their careers: experienced enough to have developed substantial expertise, but still positioned to use that experience to create further impact.

The program describes the ideal candidates as people who have enough professional experience to ask difficult questions while still having considerable time remaining in their careers to apply what they learn.

This means the Fellowship is not simply intended as recognition for past achievements. It is also intended to provide an opportunity for professional renewal, reflection, experimentation, and development.

Applicants should therefore be prepared to demonstrate not only what they have accomplished, but also how they have developed as practitioners and how additional time, resources, networks, and intellectual engagement could contribute to their future work.

The Fellowship Is for Practitioners, Not Students

The Loeb Fellowship makes an important distinction between professional practice and academic study.

It is not a student program and is not intended for people who are applying to Harvard Graduate School of Design as students.

It is also generally not intended as a traditional academic sabbatical.

Academics may potentially qualify in limited circumstances if more than 50 percent of their time is devoted to professional practice and they satisfy the other requirements. However, the program advises individuals in this situation to contact the Fellowship to discuss their eligibility.

What Does the Harvard Loeb Fellowship Application Require?

Applicants are required to submit an online application.

The standard application includes:

  1. Completed online application
  2. Three letters of recommendation
  3. Professional resume

Applicants can also submit supplemental materials, including a portfolio and other examples of their professional work.

The application is completed online through SlideRoom, and applicants are required to register before submitting their materials. Applicants are advised to answer all questions on the application form while paying attention to the suggested response lengths.

Three Letters of Recommendation Are Required

Applicants must provide three professional recommendations.

The program recommends choosing people who know the applicant and their professional work well. Potential recommenders may include:

  • Colleagues
  • Clients
  • Collaborators
  • Other individuals with substantive knowledge of the applicant’s work

The strongest recommendations are expected to come from people who can provide meaningful insight into the applicant’s professional accomplishments, abilities, character as a practitioner, and contribution to their field.

The recommendations are confidential and are not available to the applicant.

When Are Recommendation Letters Due?

Recommendation letters are due seven days after the main application deadline.

For the 2027–28 Fellowship, the recommendation deadline is:

Tuesday, January 12, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

Applicants should not wait until the final application deadline to begin communicating with their recommenders.

Once an applicant enters a recommender’s name and contact information into SlideRoom, the system sends the recommender a request. The applicant does not need to finish the entire application before the recommendation request can be triggered.

Applicants are also advised to remind recommenders to check their spam or junk folders because the request will come from SlideRoom rather than directly from the Loeb Fellowship.

What Should Be Included in the Resume?

Applicants must submit a professional resume that includes the dates of their work history.

If an applicant has earned university degrees, the resume should include:

  • Name of the educational institution
  • Full name of the degree
  • Year the degree was awarded

Applicants should avoid relying solely on academic credentials because the Loeb Fellowship emphasizes professional accomplishments and practice.

Portfolio and Supplemental Materials

Applicants may also submit a portfolio or supplemental materials demonstrating their professional work.

Examples of materials that may be submitted include:

  • Articles
  • Books
  • Videos
  • Visual representations
  • Lectures
  • Other materials that demonstrate the applicant’s work

These materials are optional, but the Fellowship strongly encourages applicants to submit up to five documents illustrating their work.

Applicants should be strategic when selecting these materials. Because the Selection Committee has limited time to review applications, supplemental materials should communicate the applicant’s work clearly and effectively rather than overwhelming reviewers with excessive information.

Is There an Application Fee?

No.

There is no fee to apply for the Harvard Loeb Fellowship.

How Does the Loeb Fellowship Selection Process Work?

The selection process involves multiple stages.

A Selection Committee reviews submitted applications. The committee consists of:

  • Three faculty members from the Graduate School of Design
  • Three Loeb Fellowship alumni
  • Two outside practitioners
  • The curator of the program

The committee initially selects approximately 20 shortlisted applicants by the end of February.

Applicants are expected to receive information about their application status by mid-March.

Shortlisted candidates may then participate in up to three separate interviews:

  1. An interview with the Curator
  2. An interview with a member of the Selection Committee
  3. A third interview with someone familiar with the program

The committee meets in mid-April to select up to 10 Fellows, with selected Fellows expected to be notified by the end of April.

The Loeb/ArtLab Fellowship

Applicants who are interested in the Loeb/ArtLab Fellowship can also indicate that interest during the application process.

The Loeb Fellowship and Harvard ArtLab have established a joint fellowship designed to support artists whose practices and research align with the objectives of the Loeb Fellowship.

The Loeb/ArtLab Fellowship is intended for innovative artists whose work focuses on improving the built and natural environment while encouraging:

  • Interdisciplinary exchange
  • Experimentation
  • Public engagement
  • Research
  • Creative development

Selected artists receive the Loeb Fellowship experience together with additional benefits connected to ArtLab, including studio space in the ArtLab building, research support, and networking opportunities through the ArtLab community.

What Are Fellows Expected to Do During the Fellowship?

The Loeb Fellowship requires Fellows to make a significant commitment to the program.

Fellows must agree to step away from significant roles with their employers and from other substantial professional responsibilities during the Fellowship year.

This includes activities such as major professional engagements, speaking commitments, and conferences.

Fellows are also required to:

  • Audit at least one GSD course per semester
  • Remain in residence in the Cambridge area while classes are in session
  • Participate in Fellowship programs
  • Take part in weekly seminars
  • Participate in weekly dinners with invited guests
  • Join fall and spring study tours
  • Participate in retreats and other activities organized by the Fellowship
  • Engage with Harvard students and faculty
  • Participate in the broader life of the Graduate School of Design
  • Make use of resources available through Harvard University and MIT

These requirements demonstrate that the Fellowship is intended to be an immersive professional and intellectual experience rather than simply a financial award or period away from work.

Fellows Develop Individual Work Plans

Each Fellow develops an individual work plan with input from program staff.

The plan can be updated throughout the Fellowship year as the Fellow’s priorities and work develop.

At the conclusion of the Fellowship, a summary of the results of the work plan is included in the program’s final report.

This individualized approach allows Fellows to use their time according to their professional interests while remaining connected to the broader objectives and activities of the program.

Can Fellows Bring Their Families?

Yes.

The Loeb Fellowship states that its resources can support families of modest size, and many Fellows bring their families to Cambridge during the Fellowship year.

The program also notes that family members can benefit from the opportunities available in Harvard and Cambridge.

Families with school-aged children should be aware that Cambridge Public Schools use a lottery system for school selection, and families should consult the relevant Cambridge Public Schools information for details.

When Does the Fellowship Year Begin?

Fellows generally arrive in mid-August, approximately one week before classes begin.

There is an orientation period of approximately three to four days before classes start, and Fellows are advised to allow time to settle into the Cambridge area.

The precise dates depend on the academic calendar for the relevant year.

When Does the Fellowship Year End?

The program officially ends on the day after commencement.

Some Fellows, particularly those with children attending schools in the area, may remain in Cambridge through the end of the school year, which is generally around the second or third week of June.

However, Fellows must leave their Fellowship housing by June 30 at the latest.

What Happens After the Fellowship?

Completion of the Loeb Fellowship does not mark the end of the relationship with the program.

The Fellowship describes itself as a lifelong connection. Graduates join a worldwide network of more than 450 alumni.

Fellows become alumni of both the Graduate School of Design and the Loeb Fellowship and can participate in the GSD alumni community and events while receiving applicable alumni benefits.

This alumni network can provide an ongoing professional connection to other practitioners working across different disciplines and geographic regions.

The Loeb Connect Alumni Program

Potential applicants who are unfamiliar with the Loeb Fellowship, the GSD, or Harvard can participate in an optional opportunity to connect directly with Loeb alumni.

The purpose of this initiative is to give prospective applicants an opportunity to have informal conversations about the Fellowship and learn more about the experience from people who have already participated.

Participation is:

  • Open to potential applicants
  • Optional
  • Not a requirement for applying
  • Not considered as part of the admissions or selection process

For individuals planning to apply for the 2027–28 class, participation should be requested by November 30, 2026.

Information Sessions for Prospective Applicants

The Loeb Fellowship is also offering two Zoom webinars for prospective applicants.

The sessions are scheduled for Monday, November 9, with one session at 8:00 a.m. ET and another at 4:00 p.m. ET.

The webinars are intended to help interested candidates learn more about the Fellowship and ask questions. The presentation will subsequently be recorded and made available on the Loeb Fellowship website together with answers to questions raised during the sessions.

Reapplying to the Harvard Loeb Fellowship

Individuals who applied in a previous year and want to apply again must submit a new application through the online system.

A new application includes the required application information and supporting materials, including:

  • Contact information
  • Application forms
  • Resume
  • Portfolio, where applicable
  • Supplemental materials, where applicable

Recommendation letters from the immediate previous application year remain available to the program. However, applicants are advised to obtain at least one new recommendation that reflects work completed during the intervening period.

Recommendation letters from earlier years will not be accepted.

Important Considerations Before Applying

Prospective applicants should carefully assess whether the Fellowship aligns with their professional circumstances before submitting an application.

The program is particularly appropriate for practitioners who:

  • Have at least eight years of professional experience
  • Are established in their fields
  • Have demonstrated leadership
  • Have a record of meaningful professional work
  • Work in areas connected to the built or natural environment
  • Are interested in broader social impact
  • Are prepared to step away from significant professional responsibilities for the Fellowship year
  • Want to reflect on their professional experience and develop new capacities
  • Are prepared to participate actively in the Harvard GSD community

Applicants should also understand that the Fellowship is not simply an academic study opportunity. It requires active participation, residence in the Cambridge area during relevant periods, coursework, seminars, study tours, dinners, retreats, and engagement with the Harvard community.

Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 Application Checklist

Before submitting an application, prospective candidates should ensure that they have prepared the necessary materials and understand the key dates.

Application materials

  • Completed online application
  • Professional resume
  • Three professional recommendation letters
  • Portfolio and/or supplemental materials, if desired
  • Relevant work samples, with up to five supplemental documents strongly encouraged

Before submission

Applicants should:

  1. Review the Fellowship’s eligibility requirements.
  2. Confirm that they have at least eight years of professional experience.
  3. Consider how their work relates to the built or natural environment and broader social impact.
  4. Prepare a clear professional resume.
  5. Identify three appropriate professional recommenders.
  6. Enter recommender information into SlideRoom early.
  7. Select strong supplemental materials that clearly demonstrate their work.
  8. Ensure digital materials are uploaded correctly.
  9. Submit the completed application before the deadline.
  10. Follow up with recommenders to ensure their letters are submitted by the separate recommendation deadline.

Key Dates at a Glance

Event Date
Loeb Connect request deadline for 2027–28 applicants November 30, 2026
Prospective applicant webinars November 9, 2026
Main application deadline January 5, 2027, 11:59 p.m. ET
Recommendation deadline January 12, 2027, 11:59 p.m. ET
Approximately 20 applicants shortlisted By end of February
Applicant status notifications Mid-March
Final selection of up to 10 Fellows Mid-April
Selected Fellows notified By end of April
Fellowship begins Mid-August
Latest housing departure June 30

The dates above are based on the information provided for the 2027–28 Fellowship cycle.

How to Apply for the Harvard Loeb Fellowship

Applicants should first carefully review the Fellowship’s application information and frequently asked questions before beginning the application.

The official application is submitted online through SlideRoom. Applicants must register on the platform and complete the required application questions.

All supplemental materials must be submitted digitally because the Selection Committee does not review hard copies. Applicants experiencing technical problems with SlideRoom are advised to first consult SlideRoom Help and, if necessary, contact the Loeb Fellowship office regarding unresolved upload problems.

CLICK HERE TO APPLY

Frequently Asked Questions About the Harvard Loeb Fellowship

Can someone who is not a designer apply?

Yes. The Fellowship has a broad definition of professional practice and has welcomed practitioners from a variety of disciplines.

Can current students apply?

No. The Fellowship is intended for practitioners with at least eight years of professional experience.

Do applicants need a university degree?

No. A completed higher-education degree is not required.

Do applicants have to be U.S. citizens?

No. International applicants are encouraged to apply.

Is there an application fee?

No. Applying to the Loeb Fellowship is free.

Are academic transcripts required?

No. Academic transcripts are not reviewed.

Are recommendation letters required?

Yes. Three professional recommendation letters are required.

When are recommendation letters due?

For the 2027–28 Fellowship, recommendations are due January 12, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET, seven days after the main application deadline.

Can applicants submit portfolios?

Yes. Portfolios and supplemental materials are optional but strongly encouraged.

Can Fellows bring their families?

Yes. The Fellowship states that its resources can support families of modest size, and many Fellows bring their families.

Do Fellows have to live in Cambridge?

Fellows are required to remain in residence in the Cambridge area while classes are in session and participate in the Fellowship’s activities.

CLICK HERE for more information about the Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28

Conclusion

The Harvard Loeb Fellowship 2027–28 provides an opportunity for experienced practitioners to step away from their regular professional responsibilities and spend a year developing new ideas, expanding their skills, engaging with Harvard’s academic and professional communities, and planning the next phase of their careers.

The Fellowship is particularly notable for its broad approach to eligibility. Applicants do not have to follow a traditional academic or professional path, and a university degree is not required. What matters is substantial professional experience, demonstrated ability, leadership potential, a commitment to supporting others, and work connected to improving the built or natural environment and creating broader social impact.

International professionals are encouraged to apply, and there is no application fee. Candidates should, however, carefully consider the Fellowship’s substantial participation requirements, including residence in Cambridge, coursework, seminars, study tours, retreats, and engagement with the Harvard Graduate School of Design community.

For professionals who meet the requirements and are considering applying, the most important date to remember is January 5, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET, when the main application closes. Recommendation letters have a separate deadline of January 12, 2027, at 11:59 p.m. ET.

The source also provides an application route through SlideRoom for the 2027–28 Loeb Fellowship.

The DIViNE Doctoral Network (Democratic Institutions and Violence Network in Europe) is offering an exciting opportunity for aspiring researchers interested in democracy, political violence, conflict, institutional change, and democratic resilience.

The network is designed to develop a new generation of interdisciplinary researchers capable of examining why political violence persists, changes, or is contained within democratic societies. It brings together leading European research institutions and international partner organizations, combining quantitative research, behavioral and experimental methods, historical and archival research, institutional theory, and policy engagement.

As part of the initiative, DIViNE plans to hire 10 PhD researchers, with two researchers associated with each of the five principal university nodes. In addition, the Political Institutions and Conflict – Max Planck Institute in Göttingen will offer one further non-MSCA PhD scholarship.

The current opportunity is an Expression of Interest (EOI) rather than the final PhD application. Interested candidates are invited to submit their expressions of interest by October 10, 2026. The formal PhD vacancy calls are expected to be published between October and November 2026, with PhD positions starting by January 2027.

What Is the DIViNE Doctoral Network?

DIViNE stands for Democratic Institutions and Violence Network in Europe.

The network addresses a central research puzzle: although democracies are generally associated with institutionalized political competition and nonviolent forms of contestation, democratic societies can still experience different forms of political violence.

These forms of violence can include:

  • Riots
  • Electoral intimidation
  • Extremist mobilization
  • Organized political violence
  • Criminal violence with political dimensions
  • State and non-state violence
  • Repression
  • Militarized responses to perceived threats

Political violence can challenge democratic institutions and norms. At the same time, governments responding to violence or perceived security threats may introduce measures that themselves create tensions with democratic principles.

Examples include:

  • Militarized policing
  • Emergency legislation
  • Selective repression
  • Expanded security measures
  • Restrictions on civil liberties
  • Institutional responses that affect impartiality or the rule of law

DIViNE seeks to examine these relationships systematically by bringing together researchers from different academic traditions and methodological backgrounds.

The Central Research Problem

A key concern of DIViNE is understanding how and why political violence persists, transforms, or becomes contained within democracies.

This involves studying both the causes and consequences of violence.

Researchers may investigate questions such as:

  • Why does political violence continue after countries democratize?
  • How do historical experiences of violence affect contemporary politics?
  • How do democratic institutions respond to violent challenges?
  • Why do some populations support or tolerate political violence?
  • How do governments respond to violent movements?
  • Can democratic reforms reduce political conflict?
  • Under what circumstances can reforms unintentionally create new incentives for violence?
  • How does militarization affect democratic institutions?
  • How can democratic institutions and civil society strengthen resilience against political violence?

The network approaches these questions from historical, institutional, behavioral, comparative, and methodological perspectives.

DIViNE PhD Positions 2026–2027

DIViNE plans to recruit:

10 PhD researchers

The researchers will be distributed across the five main university nodes, with:

  • 2 PhD researchers at the University of Amsterdam
  • 2 PhD researchers at the University of Essex
  • 2 PhD researchers at the University of Milan
  • 2 PhD researchers at Carlos III University of Madrid
  • 2 PhD researchers at Uppsala University

In addition, the Political Institutions and Conflict – Max Planck Institute in Göttingen will offer one further non-MSCA PhD scholarship.

The positions are intended for researchers whose interests align with the broader research agenda of DIViNE.

Important: This Is Currently an Expression of Interest

Prospective applicants should understand that the current announcement is not yet the final PhD vacancy application.

DIViNE is currently inviting candidates to submit an Expression of Interest.

The formal PhD vacancy calls are expected to be published:

Between October and November 2026

Formal applications will subsequently need to be submitted through the relevant DIViNE university webpages.

Therefore, submitting an expression of interest is an important preliminary step, but candidates should also monitor the relevant university websites for the official PhD vacancy announcements.

Expression of Interest Deadline

The deadline to submit the current expression of interest is:

October 10, 2026

Interested candidates should submit their expression of interest through the form provided by DIViNE.

Submit the DIViNE Expression of Interest

What Information Is Required for the Expression of Interest?

The expression of interest asks candidates to provide information in four main areas.

1. Bachelor’s and Master’s Information

Applicants will need to provide information about their:

  • Bachelor’s degree
  • Master’s degree
  • Academic background

Candidates should therefore have their relevant academic information available when completing the form.

2. Motivation and Research Idea

Applicants will be asked to explain:

  • Why they are interested in the program
  • Their proposed research idea
  • Their research question
  • Relevant literature
  • Their theoretical or substantive argument
  • Their proposed methods

This section is particularly important because it gives applicants an opportunity to demonstrate how their academic interests connect with the DIViNE research agenda.

A good research idea should be sufficiently focused to communicate a clear research question while demonstrating awareness of relevant academic debates.

3. Selected Work Package or Research Theme

Applicants will need to identify the Work Package(s) (WP) that interest them.

They will also be asked to provide a short explanation of:

  • Why they are interested in the selected theme
  • Why their research background fits the theme
  • How their proposed research connects with the selected research area

Applicants should therefore carefully examine the DIViNE research themes before selecting their preferred area.

4. Two Referees

Candidates must provide the names of two referees who will support their application.

Applicants should consider selecting referees who are familiar with their academic background and can provide relevant information about their research abilities and potential.

DIViNE’s Two Main Objectives

The Doctoral Training Network has two overarching ambitions.

Objective 1: Advance Scientific Understanding

The network aims to improve scientific understanding of:

  • Why political violence persists
  • How political violence changes
  • Why violence becomes contained in some democratic settings
  • How institutions respond to violent challenges
  • How historical experiences influence contemporary politics

Objective 2: Train a New Generation of Interdisciplinary Scholars

DIViNE also aims to train researchers who can conduct:

  • Cross-disciplinary research
  • Multi-method research
  • Scientifically rigorous research
  • Policy-relevant research
  • Research relevant to stakeholders and institutions

This means the program is not focused solely on developing theoretical academic knowledge. It also emphasizes the ability to produce research that can engage with real-world policy and institutional questions.

The Four DIViNE Research Themes

The network organizes its research around four major themes.

1. Conflict Inheritance and Legacies in Democracies

This theme investigates how historical violence continues to influence contemporary democratic politics.

Researchers examine issues such as:

  • Historical violence
  • Repression
  • Institutional legacies
  • Transitional compromises
  • Contemporary political behavior
  • Institutional functioning

A central question is how experiences from the past can continue to shape political institutions and behavior long after the original conflict has ended.

2. Democratization and Conflict Resolution

The second theme focuses on political reforms introduced during democratic transitions and their consequences for violence and reconciliation.

Potential areas of research include:

  • Transitional justice
  • Decentralization
  • Land reform
  • Territorial reform
  • Constitutional redesign
  • Power-sharing
  • Political reconciliation

The research examines whether such reforms reduce conflict, create incentives for cooperation, or sometimes generate unintended consequences.

3. Dynamics of Support for Violent Movements and Responses

The third research theme focuses on the individual and societal foundations of support for political violence.

It examines questions such as:

  • Why do people support political violence?
  • Why do some people tolerate violence?
  • How do violent organizations cultivate legitimacy?
  • How do state actors develop legitimacy for coercive responses?
  • What causes people to support or reject violent movements?

This theme places particular emphasis on the micro-foundations of political violence.

4. Democratic Resilience and Violent Stress

The fourth theme examines how democratic institutions respond when they face violent or security-related pressures.

Research can focus on:

  • Institutional design
  • Public policy
  • Civil society
  • Securitization
  • Militarization
  • Democratic resilience
  • Institutional responses to violence

A key concern is whether responses to violence strengthen democratic resilience or unintentionally create conditions that contribute to democratic erosion.

Ten Doctoral Candidate Research Themes

The network identifies ten specific research themes for doctoral candidates.

DC1 — Historical Legacies of Violence and Democratic Institutions

This research area examines the relationship between historical experiences of violence and the functioning of democratic institutions.

DC2 — Exogenous Shocks, Violent Legacies, and Democratic Resilience

This theme examines how external shocks and existing legacies of violence interact with democratic resilience.

DC3 — Endogenous Persistence of Violence After Democratization

This research area focuses on why violence can persist within countries even after democratization.

DC4 — The Unintended Consequences of Democratic Reforms

This theme investigates situations in which reforms intended to strengthen democracy or resolve conflict produce unexpected consequences.

DC5 — Institutional Reform, Violence, and Democratic Consolidation

This research examines the relationship between institutional reform, political violence, and the consolidation of democratic systems.

DC6 — Security Externalities and Post-Conflict Democratization

This theme explores security consequences associated with post-conflict democratization.

DC7 — Public Support for Political Violence in Advanced Democracies

This research area focuses on public attitudes toward political violence within established democratic settings.

DC8 — Militarization, Public Support, and Democratic Erosion in Latin America

This theme examines relationships among militarization, public attitudes, and democratic erosion in Latin American contexts.

DC9 — Democratic Decline, Political Violence, and Cycles of Repression

This research area examines interactions between democratic decline, political violence, and repression.

DC10 — Recruitment Dynamics and Behavioral Output of Violent Organizations

This theme focuses on how violent organizations recruit participants and how recruitment relates to organizational behavior.

Universities and Research Institutions in the DIViNE Network

DIViNE brings together five principal European university research environments:

  • University of Amsterdam (UvA)
  • University of Essex (UESSEX)
  • University of Milan (UMIL)
  • Carlos III University of Madrid (UC3M)
  • Uppsala University (UU)

Together, these institutions contribute complementary research expertise to the network.

The research environment combines several methodological and disciplinary approaches.

These include:

  • Quantitative conflict research
  • Behavioral research
  • Experimental methods
  • Historical research
  • Archival research
  • Institutional theory
  • Normative theory
  • Policy engagement

This interdisciplinary structure is one of the defining characteristics of the doctoral network.

Faculty and PhD Supervisors

The network includes a group of researchers who will supervise doctoral candidates across the participating institutions.

The listed faculty members are:

  • Giulia Bistagnino — University of Milan
  • Simon Chauchard — Carlos III University of Madrid
  • Ursula Daxecker — University of Amsterdam / MPI
  • Annekatrin Deglow — Uppsala University
  • Hanne Fjelde — Uppsala University
  • Ismene Gizelis — University of Essex
  • Kristian S. Gleditsch — University of Essex
  • Kathleen Klaus — Uppsala University
  • Juan Masullo — University of Milan
  • Brian Phillips — University of Essex
  • Paola Rebughini — University of Milan
  • Andrea Ruggeri — University of Milan
  • Ignacio Sánchez-Cuenca — Carlos III University of Madrid
  • Jessica Soedirgo — University of Amsterdam
  • Abbey Steele — University of Amsterdam
  • Francisco Villamil — Carlos III University of Madrid

The range of faculty expertise reflects the network’s interdisciplinary approach to studying political violence and democratic institutions.

Research Partners and PhD Research Stays

DIViNE PhD researchers will also have research stays with partner organizations associated with the network.

Partners include:

  • Action on Armed Violence (AOAV)
  • Barcelona Centre for International Affairs (CIDOB)
  • Clingendael — Netherlands Institute of International Relations
  • Fondazione Giangiacomo Feltrinelli
  • International Catalan Institute for Peace (ICIP)
  • International IDEA
  • Political Institutions and Conflict – Max Planck Institute in Göttingen

These partnerships can expose doctoral researchers to research environments beyond universities and provide opportunities to engage with organizations working on conflict, peace, governance, and international affairs.

International and Interdisciplinary Research Environment

One of the central features of DIViNE is its combination of different research methods.

Political violence is a complex phenomenon, and the network approaches it from multiple perspectives.

Quantitative Conflict Research

Quantitative methods can be used to examine patterns of conflict and political violence across countries, regions, and time periods.

Behavioral and Experimental Methods

Behavioral and experimental research can help investigate how individuals perceive political violence, institutions, security, and political movements.

Historical and Archival Research

Historical and archival approaches allow researchers to examine how past political violence, repression, and institutional arrangements influence contemporary political behavior.

Institutional and Normative Theory

The network also incorporates theoretical approaches to understanding democratic institutions, political authority, legitimacy, and institutional responses to violence.

Policy Engagement

The program aims to produce research that is not only scientifically rigorous but also relevant to policymakers and other stakeholders.

Mobility Requirements for PhD Researchers

An important requirement applies to researchers recruited through the Marie Skłodowska-Curie Actions (MSCA) framework.

PhD researchers recruited to the project must satisfy the relevant MSCA mobility requirements.

In particular, they must not have:

Resided or worked for more than one year in the country of the institution where they are enrolled.

Applicants should therefore carefully assess their residence and employment history before applying.

The doctoral program will also involve mobility across institutions and partners within the network.

This means that doctoral researchers should be prepared for an international and mobile research experience rather than remaining exclusively at a single institution throughout the program.

When Will the PhD Positions Start?

The DIViNE announcement states that PhD positions are expected to start by January 2027.

The formal vacancy calls are expected to be published between:

October and November 2026

Candidates interested in the positions should therefore monitor the relevant DIViNE university webpages after submitting their expression of interest.

How to Prepare for the DIViNE PhD Opportunity

Prospective candidates can begin preparing before the formal vacancies are published.

Step 1: Review Your Academic Background

Prepare information about your:

  • Bachelor’s degree
  • Master’s degree
  • Research experience
  • Academic interests
  • Relevant coursework
  • Previous research projects

Step 2: Identify Your Research Area

Review the four major research themes and ten doctoral research themes.

Consider which area most closely matches your interests.

Step 3: Develop a Research Idea

Prepare a preliminary research idea that includes:

  • A clear research question
  • Relevant literature
  • A potential argument
  • Possible research methods
  • A clear connection to political violence and democratic institutions

Step 4: Consider Your Preferred Work Package

Identify the Work Package or research theme that interests you most and think about why your background makes you a good fit.

Step 5: Identify Two Referees

Choose two academic referees who can support your application.

Contact them in advance so they are aware of your interest in the program.

Step 6: Check MSCA Mobility Eligibility

Carefully examine your residence and employment history in relation to the country where you intend to enroll.

This is particularly important because the mobility requirement can affect eligibility.

Step 7: Monitor the Formal Vacancy Calls

Remember that the current form is an Expression of Interest.

The formal PhD vacancies are expected to be published between October and November 2026.

Why Consider the DIViNE Doctoral Network?

DIViNE offers an opportunity to develop doctoral research within a large European research network focused on important questions surrounding democracy and political violence.

Potential areas of academic development include:

  • Developing advanced research skills
  • Working across disciplinary boundaries
  • Learning multiple research methods
  • Conducting comparative political research
  • Engaging with historical and contemporary political violence
  • Collaborating with researchers across Europe
  • Participating in research stays with partner organizations
  • Developing policy-relevant research
  • Building an international academic network
  • Working with researchers specializing in political institutions, conflict, violence, and democratic resilience

The network’s combination of university research and external partners can also provide exposure to different approaches to producing and applying research.

Important Dates for the DIViNE PhD Network

January 2027 PhD positions expected to start by this time

How to Submit Your Expression of Interest

Candidates interested in being considered for the DIViNE doctoral network should complete the online Expression of Interest form.

The form asks applicants for:

  1. Bachelor’s and Master’s information
  2. Motivation and research idea
  3. Research question
  4. Relevant literature
  5. Arguments and methods
  6. Selected Work Package or research theme
  7. Motivation and fit with the selected theme
  8. Names of two referees

Expression of Interest Deadline

October 10, 2026

Submit the DIViNE Expression of Interest Form

Candidates should also monitor the official DIViNE and participating university websites for the formal vacancy announcements.

Frequently Asked Questions About the DIViNE PhD Network

What does DIViNE stand for?

DIViNE stands for Democratic Institutions and Violence Network in Europe.

How many PhD researchers will DIViNE recruit?

The network plans to hire 10 PhD researchers, with two researchers associated with each of its five principal university nodes.

An additional non-MSCA PhD scholarship will be offered by the Political Institutions and Conflict – Max Planck Institute in Göttingen.

What is the current application?

The current opportunity is an Expression of Interest, not the final PhD vacancy application.

When will the formal PhD vacancies be published?

The formal calls are expected to be published between October and November 2026.

When will the PhD positions start?

The positions are expected to start by January 2027.

What is the Expression of Interest deadline?

The deadline is October 10, 2026.

What research topics does DIViNE cover?

The network focuses on political violence and democratic institutions, including historical legacies, democratization, conflict resolution, public support for violence, militarization, democratic resilience, repression, and democratic decline.

Are multiple research methods used?

Yes. The network combines quantitative conflict research, behavioral and experimental methods, historical and archival inquiry, institutional and normative theory, and policy engagement.
